slides.title: What a Clinical Trial Actually Is
bullets: A prospective study that assigns an intervention to evaluate its effect on health outcomes
Follows a predefined protocol from start to finish
Understanding phases, design and limitations underlies every credible science conversation

slides.title: Phase I Through IV, In Order
bullets: Phase I tests safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetics in a small group, establishing a safe dose range
Phase II expands to patients to explore preliminary efficacy and refine dosing
Phase III is the pivotal trial, powered to confirm efficacy and safety against a standard comparator
Phase IV happens post-launch, in larger and more diverse real-use populations, catching rare or long-term effects

slides.title: Four Pillars of a Credible Trial
bullets: Randomization spreads baseline differences evenly across treatment arms
Blinding, single, double or triple, reduces expectation bias in patients, investigators and assessors
The control group, placebo or active comparator, is the reference the effect is measured against
Sample size is calculated upfront to detect a clinically relevant difference

slides.title: Who Was Actually Studied
bullets: Inclusion and exclusion criteria define which population the results can be extrapolated to
Strict criteria, young patients, no comorbidities, no polypharmacy, can show efficacy under ideal conditions
That same effect may not reproduce in the real, heterogeneous patients a clinician sees
This is the efficacy-versus-effectiveness gap that connects directly to real-world evidence

slides.title: Knowing the Pivotal Trial Cold
bullets: Sample size, comparator, inclusion criteria, endpoints and follow-up are not academic trivia
They let an MSL answer who does this population resemble
They let an MSL answer why this comparator and how robust is this result

takeaway.title: Trial phases and design choices determine what a result can and cannot claim
bullets: Each phase answers a different question, from first-in-human safety to real-world use
Randomization, blinding, a control group and a pre-calculated sample size make a result trustworthy
Strict trial populations create an efficacy-to-effectiveness gap that real-world data helps close
